Rhodes New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Rodos, Greece

Not demolished. Romaniot Jews are documented on Rhodes from the 2nd century BCE, with a 12th-century community of about 400 per Benjamin of Tudela; a synagogue was built under the Knights of St. John (1309-1522), though an earthquake destroyed the Jewish quarter in 1481-82. Following the 1502 expulsion, Spanish and Portuguese refugees plus 40 Sultan-relocated Salonika families formed a predominantly Sephardi community renowned for its rabbis and rabbinical institutions; a second synagogue followed in 1577. R. Moshe Israel served as Chief Rabbi from 1714-36, making Rhodes a notable Torah-study center. An 1837 epidemic killed 10 Jews; subsequent earthquakes (1851, 1863-64), an 1855 explosion, and fires (1865, 1867) caused severe damage. Population reached 2,401 by 1884; boys' (1899) and girls' (1902) schools opened with Alliance Israelite support. Population peaked at 4,500 (of 14,100 total) by 1912, active Zionist groups formed in the 1920s, and numbers fell to 2,200 by 1940 and 1,900 by 1943 amid deportations. Postwar survivors numbered 200 by 1947, dwindling to just 50 by 1959. This newer cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 16th century.
